web_evidence.title: Race Man, Organization Man, Invisible Man — The Twilight of the Middle Class
web_evidence.note: Andrew Hoberek’s Princeton University Press study explicitly contrasts Ellison’s first-person narration with Wilson’s “straightforwardly omniscient narration,” establishing the novel’s controlling third-person mode.

web_evidence.title: Constructed Identities: A Chronotopic Reading of The Great Gatsby, The Man in the Gray Flannel Suit, and Mad Men
web_evidence.note: This University of Bergen thesis analyzes the novel’s overall narrative construction, describes its narration as centered on Tom’s flashbacks, and quotes third-person prose from the opening through the ending.

web_evidence.title: Conformity and Literature of the 1950s — The Man in the Gray Flannel Suit excerpt
web_evidence.note: The multi-paragraph opening excerpt narrates Tom and Betsy externally as “they,” then renders Tom’s thoughts through a third-person frame.

person_note: The controlling voice is nonparticipating omniscient third-person narration, frequently focalized through Tom and sometimes other characters. The sustained event passages q00911–q00912 independently display that pattern, and the scholarly whole-book evidence explicitly identifies Wilson’s mode as omniscient. First-person language in q00905–q00906 is dialogue, while q00916 and q00919 explicitly embed Tom’s “I/me” inside thoughts framed as “he thought” or “Tom thought”; none constitutes an autonomous first-person section. Targeted searches found no epistolary, framed, or alternating-person structure. Although an authorized full-book excerpt was not openly readable, the explicit Tier B account, a second academic structural analysis, and corroborating opening/interior prose leave no material uncertainty.
